title: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
eyebrow: Frontend foundation · Meaning, appearance, and behavior
summary: Learn the three core browser languages by building one small page: HTML gives content meaning and structure, CSS controls presentation and layout, and JavaScript adds behavior when the page needs to react or change.
prerequisites: How the Web Works is helpful because it explains how these files reach the browser, but this guide explains the page-building concepts it uses.
learningOutcomes: Look at a page requirement and decide whether HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or a combination should handle it.
Explain elements, CSS rules and the cascade, the DOM, events, state, and browser APIs in the context of a working page.
Build an accessible component that starts with native browser behavior and adds styling or JavaScript only where the requirement needs it.

heroVisual.title: One page, three different responsibilities
heroVisual.caption: The layers cooperate, but keeping their jobs clear makes the page easier to understand, change, test, and recover when something fails.

nodes.label: HTML · meaning and structure
nodes.detail: Defines headings, paragraphs, links, buttons, forms, images, sections, and the relationships between them.

nodes.label: CSS · presentation and layout
nodes.detail: Controls visual styling, spacing, sizing, layout, responsive adaptation, and visual states.

nodes.label: JavaScript · behavior and change
nodes.detail: Responds to events, calls browser or network APIs, keeps application state, and changes the page when needed.

sections.title: 1. Start with one page and separate its three jobs
sections.summary: Before syntax, learn what each language is responsible for. That decision prevents many later accessibility, maintenance, and performance problems.

blocks.text: Imagine a small article card with a heading, a description, and a link to read more. HTML identifies those things and their meaning. CSS can make the card two columns on a wide container and one column on a narrow one. If the card later needs live filtering, saved preferences, or data loaded after an interaction, JavaScript can coordinate that behavior.

blocks.code:
How the Web Works

Follow one request from browser to server and back.

Read the guide
blocks.explanation: The article element identifies a self-contained piece of content, h2 gives it a heading, p is descriptive text, and a is a real link to another location. No styling is required for those meanings to exist.
CSS selects the article and link and changes presentation: grid layout, spacing, padding, border, and font weight. It does not change the link into a different kind of control.

blocks.prompt: A control should take the user to another page. Which language should provide that basic capability first?
blocks.answer: HTML, with a real link such as an <a href="…"> element.
blocks.explanation: Navigation is already a native browser capability. CSS can style the link and JavaScript can enhance navigation when a real requirement calls for it, but neither should replace the correct HTML meaning without a reason.

sections.title: 2. HTML tells the browser what the content is
sections.summary: HTML is markup: elements and attributes describe content, relationships, controls, and document structure so browsers and assistive technology can understand them.

visual.title: Build meaning from the document outward
visual.caption: Start with the content's job, then choose the element whose built-in meaning and behavior matches it.

nodes.label: Document structure
nodes.detail: Headings, main content, navigation, sections, articles, lists, and other landmarks organize information.

nodes.label: Content meaning
nodes.detail: Paragraphs, emphasis, tables, figures, time values, and other elements communicate what the content represents.

nodes.label: Native interaction
nodes.detail: Links, buttons, forms, inputs, details, and other controls bring browser behavior and accessibility semantics with them.

nodes.label: Attributes
nodes.detail: Values such as href, type, name, required, alt, and autocomplete add information or configure behavior.

blocks.text: An HTML element usually has a defined purpose and behavior. Choosing <button> for an action or <a href> for navigation is more than a naming preference: the browser already knows how those controls should participate in keyboard navigation, activation, accessibility APIs, and other platform behavior. Semantic HTML means choosing elements for what the content or control is, not simply for how you want it to look.

items.title: Link
items.summary: Moves to a resource or location.
items.avoidWhen: Do not use a link with a fake URL for an in-page action.

items.title: Button
items.summary: Triggers an action in the current context.
items.whenToUse: Submit, open, close, save, toggle, or run another action.
items.avoidWhen: Do not make a clickable div imitate a button.

items.title: Label and input
items.summary: A form control needs a programmatic name so the user knows what information is requested.
items.whenToUse: Use a visible label whenever possible.
items.avoidWhen: Placeholder text is not a replacement for a label.

blocks.title: Heading levels describe hierarchy, not font size
blocks.body: Use h1, h2, h3, and later levels to represent nested sections. Change their appearance with CSS instead of choosing a heading level merely because its default size looks right.

sections.title: 3. CSS turns rules into presentation
sections.summary: CSS lets several rules describe how HTML should look. The browser matches those rules, resolves conflicts, calculates values, lays out boxes, and paints them.

blocks.explanation: .guide-card and .guide-card a are selectors: they describe which elements a rule can apply to. Inside each rule, properties such as background and padding name what is being set, and values such as white or 1rem supply the setting.

blocks.text: More than one CSS declaration can try to set the same property on the same element. The cascade is the browser's conflict-resolution process. It considers where a declaration came from, importance, cascade layers, selector specificity, scoping proximity where applicable, and source order to decide which declaration wins. You do not need to memorize every tie-breaker before using CSS, but you do need the mental model: the browser is resolving competing rules, not randomly ignoring one.

rows: Normal flow
Content should follow the document's natural block/inline reading order.
Let content create the page before adding a layout system.
Flexbox
Items need alignment or distribution mainly along one dimension.
A row or column whose children share available space.
Grid
Rows and columns need to work together.
A two-dimensional set of tracks and areas.
Container queries
A reusable component should adapt to the space its container gives it.
Ask about the component's available context rather than only the whole viewport.
blocks.caption: Choose a layout mechanism from the relationship between the content, not from habit

blocks.explanation: After the basic card works, container-type makes it eligible for size queries. The @container rule changes the card to two columns only when its own inline size is wider than 36rem. cqi is a container-query length unit; here it helps the heading scale with the container while clamp() keeps explicit minimum and maximum sizes.

blocks.prompt: Two CSS rules set different colors on the same link. Is one rule automatically 'broken'?
blocks.explanation: CSS is designed to combine many rules. The cascade decides which applicable declaration wins. Debug by inspecting which declarations match and why one has priority instead of assuming the browser ignored CSS.

sections.title: 4. JavaScript reacts when the page needs behavior or changing state
sections.summary: JavaScript is a programming language. In a browser it can listen for events, calculate values, call browser APIs, request data, and change the document or application state.

visual.title: A simple browser interaction
visual.caption: Events tell code that something happened; state represents what the application needs to remember; rendering or DOM changes make the result visible.

nodes.label: Event
nodes.detail: Something happens, such as a click, form submit, timer, or network result.

nodes.label: Handler
nodes.detail: JavaScript runs code registered to respond to that event.

nodes.label: State or calculation
nodes.detail: The code determines what the application should now know or do.

nodes.label: Visible effect
nodes.detail: The document, focus, URL, stored data, network request, or another browser capability changes.

blocks.text: The browser exposes the page to JavaScript through objects and APIs. The DOM, or Document Object Model, is the object representation of the document: elements become nodes JavaScript can find, inspect, and change. An event is a notification that something happened. State is the minimum information the application needs to remember so it can determine the current interface or behavior.

blocks.explanation: querySelector finds the button in the DOM. addEventListener registers a function for the click event. The function reads the current theme state from a data attribute, calculates the opposite value, and writes the new value back so CSS can present the corresponding theme.

items.title: Events
items.summary: Notifications such as click, input, submit, keydown, load, or a custom application event.

items.title: State
items.summary: Information that must persist long enough to determine what the application should currently show or do.
items.whenToUse: Keep one clear owner for each state value and derive other values when possible.

items.title: Browser APIs
items.summary: Capabilities supplied by the browser rather than by the JavaScript language itself, such as the DOM, Fetch, storage, history, media, and timers.

items.title: Effects
items.summary: Work that changes or communicates with something outside a pure calculation, such as a network request, timer, DOM mutation, or storage write.
items.whenToUse: Keep effects focused and clean up long-lived subscriptions or in-flight work when their owner ends.

blocks.title: JavaScript is powerful, not automatically necessary
blocks.body: If HTML or CSS already provides the required behavior, replacing it with custom JavaScript can add download, execution, failure, accessibility, and maintenance costs without adding user value.

sections.title: 5. Build the useful baseline first, then enhance it
sections.summary: A page is more resilient when meaning and core interaction exist before optional presentation or scripting is layered on top.

items.title: Describe the user's task
items.explanation: State what the person must understand or accomplish without naming a framework or implementation yet.
items.result: The requirement is about the outcome instead of a favorite tool.

items.title: Choose HTML that already matches the task
items.explanation: Create a meaningful reading order and use native links, buttons, inputs, details, and other elements where they fit.
items.result: The page has a usable structural baseline.

items.title: Add CSS for presentation and adaptation
items.explanation: Improve hierarchy, layout, spacing, responsive behavior, states, and visual comfort without changing the underlying meaning.
items.result: The interface adapts while its semantics stay stable.

items.title: Add JavaScript for requirements the platform baseline does not satisfy
items.explanation: Introduce application state, asynchronous data, coordinated interaction, or other behavior only where it produces needed capability.
items.result: The script has a clear reason to exist.

items.title: Test the complete experience
items.explanation: Use keyboard, pointer, touch, zoom, text spacing, reduced motion, errors, slow networks, and long content where applicable.
items.result: The layers work together under real conditions.

blocks.title: Progressive enhancement
blocks.body: Progressive enhancement means starting with a functional baseline and layering richer capabilities on top when the platform and context support them. It is a reliability strategy, not a rule that pages should look plain.

sections.title: 6. Responsive design means the content keeps working as its context changes
sections.summary: A robust interface does not merely shrink. It reflows, reprioritizes, wraps, and sometimes changes composition while preserving meaning and access to controls.

rows: Narrow container
Reflow into a clear primary sequence and wrap content/actions.
Identity, meaning, current task, and required actions.
More available space
Add useful side-by-side context only when it reduces effort.
Readable line length and obvious hierarchy.
Zoom or larger text spacing
Reflow instead of clipping, overlapping, or hiding information.
All content and controls.
Reduced motion preference
Remove or greatly reduce nonessential motion.
State changes and meaning through non-motion cues.
Different input methods
Keep focus visible and targets operable by keyboard, touch, pointer, and assistive technology.
Equivalent task completion.
blocks.caption: Responsive behavior follows content and task pressure, not a list of device brands

blocks.title: Breakpoints are evidence that the current composition needs to change
blocks.body: Add a media or container breakpoint where content no longer fits or reads well. A device model is not the reason; the content relationship is.

items: Prefer natural flow, wrapping, minmax(), auto-fit, and intrinsic sizing before adding many breakpoints.
Use logical properties when the layout should support different writing directions.
Keep visual order aligned with reading and keyboard focus order.
Do not use color or motion as the only way to communicate a state.
Test narrow layouts, both orientations, zoom, text spacing, long translations, and realistic content.

sections.title: 7. Put the model together with one disclosure component
sections.summary: A small native disclosure shows why choosing the platform capability first can remove code while improving resilience.

blocks.code:
What is the DOM?

The browser's object representation of the document.
blocks.explanation: details and summary already define a disclosure control. The browser supplies open/closed state, keyboard activation, and native semantics. The paragraph is the content revealed when the details element is open.
CSS improves visual grouping and target comfort but leaves the disclosure behavior owned by the native HTML control.

blocks.prompt: Do you need JavaScript just to make this one details/summary disclosure open and close?
blocks.explanation: The HTML element already provides that behavior. Add JavaScript only if a later requirement genuinely needs coordination or behavior the native element does not provide, such as synchronizing several disclosures with application state.

items: HTML communicates the content and native interaction correctly before styling.
CSS changes presentation without creating fake semantics.
JavaScript has a named behavior or state requirement before it is added.
Loading, empty, error, disabled, and success states are designed when the component can enter them.
The component remains understandable at zoom, with keyboard navigation, and when content is longer than expected.

glossary.definition: HyperText Markup Language, the web markup language used to describe document content, structure, and native controls.
Choosing HTML elements because their defined meaning and behavior match the content or task.
Cascading Style Sheets, the language used to describe presentation and layout for structured documents such as HTML.
The CSS conflict-resolution process that decides which applicable declarations win when multiple rules set the same property.
A programming language commonly used in browsers to react to events, coordinate state, call APIs, and change application behavior.
The Document Object Model, the browser's object representation of the document that APIs and scripts can inspect and change.
A notification that something happened, such as a click, input, submit, timer, or network-related result.
Information an application needs to remember so it can determine its current behavior or interface.
A capability supplied by the browser environment to code, such as the DOM, Fetch, History, Storage, media, or timers.
Starting with a functional baseline and adding richer supported capabilities without making the baseline unusable.
